TIMELY WARNING
GIVEN BY HEALTH
OFFICER LOCKE
Dr. Locke, Health Officer of Mason
County Has (lven to the Fulillc a
Very Timely Warning and It
Should He Heeded.
Influenza Is a crowded disease.
Therefore, keoi yourself and faintly
away from, crowds.
Influenza spreads mostly by
Inhaling some of the tiny troplets of
germladen mucous sprayed into the air
when earless people sneeze or cough
without using a handkerchief.
Therefore, cover up each sneeze or cough.
Every person attacked by the
disease should at once go to his home
for the safety of the community, to his
Isolated room for the safety of his
family, and to his bed under the care
of a physician, for his own welfare,
moving the bowels freely until the
doctor arrives.

If not a doctor or attendant on the
alck, stay and keep your family In
your own freely ventilated home.
Wear a well adjusted mask If you
must go Into possibly infected places,
and wash the hands and face and
cleanse the nose and throat with a
warm salt solution as soon as you get
home. Physicians and nurses should
be even more exacting about these
precautions, changing and boiling the
mask every two or three hours.
The State Board, the Public Health
Service and your own local Health
Board will assist in every voy
possible, In protecting you. but their chief
reliance in doing this must be the
physicians and volunteer practical
nurses of each community in getting

relief to you.
We repeat for the purpose of
emphasizing it, that Influenza Is a crowd
disease keep away from crowds.
You will greatly aid in the control
and in preventing the spread of
influenza by observing these simple
Injunctions. J. S. LOCKE,
Health Officer

UNDER CONTROL
Health Officer Promises Everything
Will Open up Soon if Present
Conditions Continue.
Although there are many Spanish
influenza cases in town at the present
time, the number of new cases is
steadily decreasing and it is an
evident fact that the new cases are all
much milder in form than the first
ones.
The rumor that school would open
Monday and that there would be
services at the churches Sunday is false,
according to Dr. Simpkins; but if the
present good conditions continue to
prevail it is probable that everything
will be opened some time next week.

The fact that Glasgow has been
lightly hit with the dread menace in
comparison to other towns of this size
is due to the vigilance of the board
of health. Schools, churches, saloons,
Red Cross rooms have been closed for
nearly three weeks and as all social
meetings were prohibited fewer cases
and fewer deaths have resulted than
in any town of this size in the state.

The local board is again in the
midst of a tremendous amount of
work due to the classifying of the
latest registrants. Volunteers are
wanted who can give a part of their
time to the government in assisting
the board.

DR. O. M. LANSTRUM VISITS GLASGOW, AS
REPRESENTATIVE OF STATE BOARD OF HEALTH:
HELPING TO STAMP OUT EPIDEMIC.

On his way to Henela, where he
has been summoned for conference by
the secretary of the state board of
health, Dr. Oscar M. Lanstrum,
Republican candidate for United States
senator, who has been touring
northern Montana by auto helping stamp
out the Spanish influenza epidemic
stopped in Glasgow Monday evening.
During his visit here Dr. Lanstrum
consulted with Drs. Simpkins and
Smith regarding the situation in
Glasgow and made several calls on local
cases. Upon being advised that the
situation was very well in hand here
Dr. Lanstrum continued on his way
to Nashua, the same evening, where
he had been called on special request
for aid.

Dr. Lanstrum has been doing a
wonderful work. Since leaving Helena,
where he volunteered his services to
the state board of health, before
reaching Glasgow he had traveled
more than 1000 miles and had visited
two score towns and attended victims
of the influenza in eight counties and
one in Canada, just over the boundary
from Hill county.
As a result of his trip hundreds of
men and women have been given
instruction for fighting the epidemic,
and the possibilities of its spreading
has been lessened in a large
territory in northern Montana, where there
are no resident physicians.

The scarcity of physicians is one
of the problems which confronts the
authorities in the fight that is
being made on the disease, as so many
of the Montana doctors have gone to
war. During his trip Dr. Lanstrum
was able to locate five graduated
physicians, who had retired from
practice, and induced them to resume their
proefssion during the epidemic. They
were all sent to communities where
physicians were sorely needed.
; In towns where doctors are located
Dr. Lanstrum consulted with them
and attended any cases they desired
him to see. In other places he
instructed nurses, teachers, Red Cross
workers and public spirited titizens
in how to care for any who might
contract influenza and how to
prevent it from spreading. Local stores
were given information as to what
remedies to carry for treatment of
Spanish influenza.

counties, but so well was his work
done that when these counties were

through Blaine, Phillips, Valley,
Sheridan and Richland counties, but
before this work could be completed a
telegram from Dr. Cogswell

ADOPTED B I CITI
Physicians Take New
Measures to Combat Epidemic of
Spanish Influenza 'in City;
Open Air Meetings Banned,
Whereas, the Spanish Influenza
epidemic continues to exist in
Albuquerque, constantly endangering the
lives and health of the inhabitants,
and
Whereas, the board of health of the
city of Albuquerque, in open meeting
held on this 16th day of October,
1 9 1 S. is unanimously of the opinion
that additional and more stringent
rules should be adopted and enforced,
providing for further effort ' to stop
the spread of the disease; now
therefore, Be it resolved, by the board of
health as follows: That the following
additional rules and regulations are
hereby adopted and provided by the
board of health and the city
.commission is hereby requested to see that
the same are properly enforced:
1. That nil kinds of public open air

gatherings be and hereby are
prohibited until further order of the
board. Residents of the city of
Albuquerque are requested not to violate
the spirit of this regulation by going
outside of the city limits and holding
o- participating In puh'ic gatherings
of any ki$d, held either indoors or
outdoors. This rule relates lo
religious services, concerts, lodge meetings
and othsr affairs attracting a number
of people nnd not essential to
carrying on the War.
2. In view of the infectious t aturc
of Spanish influenza it i-, ordered by
the board that insofir as possible all
funerals and funeral services shall be
private. For their own protection
and the protection of other persons
people are urged not to attend
funerals. 3. Physicians wi her eby re wired
to require patients to remain at home,
under supervision, who develop colds

running temperature, which in their
opinion are possibly incipient cases of
Spanish influenza and likely to later
develop into that disease. Tills rule
Is for the protection of the patient
himself as well as the public at large.
4. The attention of physicians is
again called to the necessity to
report immediately to the city
physician nil cases or suspected cases of
Spanish influenza. The board
recommends that physicians failing to . so
report such cases be cited to appear
in police court and that the ordinance
relating to violation of this rule be
strictly enforced with either fine or
imprisonment or both.

5. The board hereby specifies three
days as a minimum length of time
during which a Spanish influenza
patient must remain quarantined in his
own home, following the resumption
of a continued normal temperature.
6. Spanish influenza signs, posted
by the city health officer, must not
be removed by private citizens. The
board recommends the strict
enforcement of the penal clause of the
ordinance governing this matter.
7. The board herehy orders that
hereafter no fumigation of infected
premises shall be done by private
citizens, but that the same shall be done
under the direction of the city
physician, city health officer or some one
designated by either of them. The
cost for such fumigation shall be as
provided by ordinance.

The above resolutions were unani
mously adopted last night at a joint
meeting of the city commission and
the board of health. Strict enforce
ment of regulations was the keynote
of the meeting and all physicians of
the hoard concurred In the opinion of
the necessity for co-operatlon by the
public.
Don t get panicky ' was tne auvice
of the board individually and
collectively, to the public. The physicians
deelare that while the epidemic is
general still nothing is to be gained
by a panicky condition at this time.

Calm obedience to physicians' orders
is the saving action. Both members
of the board of health and the city
officials agreed that a physician
should be called at the first step when
Influenza is suspected.
George II. Peck, city health officer,
reported last night that a total of 394
cases of the disease have been
reported to the city physician. The city
physician reported that thus far
thirty-four deaths have resulted from
the disease in the city.
It was decided by the board that
the Red Cross shop, for the sale of
second hand articles, shall be closed
during the epidemic and that the Red
Cross shall be, requested to
discontinue distribution of yarn and the
acceptance of old clothing.

The "Transconlincntay Motor
Express" of the Goodyear Tire and
Rubber company, consisting of three huge
motor trucks which are traveling from
San Fianclsco to Boston on the
second lap of a round-trip journey, spent
yesterday In Albuquerque. The trucks
were adorned with Fourth Liberty
Loan posters. A big Packard
touring car escorts the trucks during their
trans-continental rambles.
M. D. Scott, manager of the
AkronBoston motor truck line on which
two of the trucks operate regularly,
is in charge of the tour and is
accompanied by Ferris R. Miller,
publicity agent for the Goodyear
company. The drivers nre Harry Apple,
Harry Smeltzer, Paul Dies. Howard
Smeltzer, Dent Webb and Carl
Cosgrove. The object of the expedition Is to
demonstrate the feasibility of motor

truck hauling. On their first trip
to San Francisco, the trucks carried
a load of aeroplane tires for the
government and on the return trip they
are carrying six tons of baled cotton.
The trucks left Boston early In
September and arrived In San Francisco
September 21.
Of peculiar interest are the trips of
the trucks. These are pneumatic and
are said to be the largest ever made.
The front tires measures 38 by 7 and
the rear tires 44 by 10 inches. The
rear tires weigh about 200 pounds
and require 140 pounds air pressure.

The drivers are divided two to each
car, each driving six hours a day.
Sleeping compartments which will
accommodate two men each, are
carried with each car.
The caravan left yesterday
afternoon for Santa Fe.
ALLEGED SLAYER OF
ZUNI MOUNTAIN MAN
CAPTURED BY ARMIJO
Sheriff P. J. Armijo of Valencia
county arrived in the city yesterday
morning with a prisoner supposed to
be the murderer of Ben Wales, a Zuni
Mountain rancher, who was known as
the S5una Mountain Terror.
Wales was found dead the latter
part of last February by some hunters
in the mountains. He was laying on
his cot in his hut with four bullet
holes in his body.

Officers took up the, trail and have
been on the lookout for the captured
man and his accomplice, who is
supposed to be Jack Brown.
The sheriff did not give the name
of his prisoner and said that he was
captured after a hard chase over the
mountains. The prisoner showed
signs of a hard chase as he looked
haggard and worn after months of
foraging in the hills existing on what
food stuffs he could find without
showing himself. He looked to be
about 21 years old. .

Officer Armijo left yesterday
afternoon to deliver his captive to the
authorities of Valencia county.

88th Division
On Front Lines
The 88th Division of the United
States Army, named the Hunhusker
division, n.nd made up largely of
soldiers from the northwest, which left
Camp Dodge, Iowa, on August 8, now
is on the battleline in France, accord
ing to Captain George Milan Hunt,
who arrived in Minneapolis today
with First Lieutenant Harold IX
Krafft.

Captain Hunt loft. France Oct. 1,
and the 88th Division, he, said, went
into the front line trenches on Oct. 5.
Thousands of Minnesotans, North
and South Dakotans and Iowans were
sent to the 88th Divisions in the first
draft.

located in a quiet sector," said Captain
Hunt. "Considerable gas and high
explosive shells are being sent over
the American lines, but there is no
aggressive action in that sector."

the division.
